title: Legal Significance of Records and Never Falsifying

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the legal significance of medical records and their role as evidence.
- Recognize that care must never be falsely documented, backdated, or recorded as performed when it was not.
- Describe record integrity and the practices that preserve it.
- Apply correct procedures for corrections, late entries, and amendments without altering the original record.
- Escalate requests to falsify, alter, or backdate documentation according to policy and within scope of practice.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A medical record is like a report card for a patient's health: it is an official written record of what happened, and because it is official, it can be shown to a judge or others who need to know the truth.

### Question 2

Think of the record like a referee's written notes during a game: they are written down as things happen so that later, if there is a question, the notes can show what really occurred.

### Question 3

The health record is like an official diary that can be shared with important grown-ups — judges, insurance companies, and government reviewers — when they need to know what happened.

### Question 4

Integrity means the record has not been secretly changed or erased — like a sealed time capsule that still holds exactly what was put inside.

### Question 5

Writing things down right away is like taking a photo while you are still looking at the scene — the sooner you record it, the more accurate the picture.

### Question 6

Falsifying is telling a lie in writing — putting down something that did not really happen, like writing you finished homework you never started.

### Question 7

You should only write down what you really saw or did — like a witness who only tells the judge what they actually observed.

### Question 8

Backdating is like writing yesterday's date on today's homework to make it look like you finished it on time — it hides when the work was really done.

### Question 9

If you write the wrong date, it is like giving a fake alibi — it makes people trust something that is not really true.

### Question 10

Your health record is like a report about you that you are allowed to read and get a copy of, so you can check it is correct.

### Question 11

Use the real date, like writing today's date on a letter you are writing right now — not some other day you wish it were.

### Question 12

If you make a mistake, you fix it in a way that still lets people see what was there first — like crossing out neatly instead of scribbling it away forever.

### Question 13

Writing the facts is like reporting what your eyes saw instead of what you guessed — facts can be checked, guesses cannot.

### Question 14

The record is valuable because it is written down right when things happen — like a referee writing notes during the game instead of remembering them a month later.

### Question 15

If you did something but wrote nothing down, it is like doing homework but never turning it in — no one can see you actually did it.

### Question 16

Writing that no one can read is like a map with smudged roads — it cannot guide anyone, and it might send them the wrong way.

### Question 17

Signing and dating your work is like writing your name on a team project so everyone knows who did which part and when.

### Question 18

This rule is like a lock on a diary that stops anyone from sneaking in and changing or ripping out the pages.

### Question 19

Even if a grown-up tells you to write something untrue, you say no and tell someone who can help — because writing lies is never okay.

### Question 20

If you forgot to write something down, write it now with today's real date and say it is a late note — you do not pretend you wrote it yesterday.

### Question 21

An accurate record is like a correct recipe — if a step is wrong, the next person following it could make a serious mistake.

### Question 22

Contemporaneous means writing it down right away, like noting the score while the game is still happening.

### Question 23

If a report about you has a mistake, there is a fair way to ask for it to be fixed — like asking a teacher to correct a wrong grade through the right steps.

### Question 24

Only write down things that truly happened, like only listing chores you actually did — not chores you only planned to do.

### Question 25

The health record is like a report card, a receipt, and a diary all in one — it helps with health, bills, and proving what happened.

### Question 26

If you see a mistake in the official notes, you tell a trusted supervisor so it can be fixed the right way — you do not scribble over it or keep quiet.

### Question 27

Even if a boss asks, you do not put a fake earlier date on a form — you politely say no and ask for help from a supervisor.

### Question 28

If you forgot to jot down a number, write it down now with today's real time and a note that it happened earlier — never fake the time.

### Question 29

You cannot just rewrite a doctor's findings because someone asks — there is a proper way to ask for a correction, like filling out a request instead of erasing the answer.

### Question 30

Using white-out on a record is like scratching out the answer on a test so no one can ever see what you first wrote — it looks like you are hiding something.

### Question 31

Fix a wrong number the way your teacher wants — cross it out neatly and write the right one — so everyone can still see what it said before.

### Question 32

Good notes are like a clear receipt — if someone asks what happened, you can show exactly what you did and when.

### Question 33

Writing about care before it happens is like filling in a weather forecast as if it already happened — it is not the truth yet.

### Question 34

If there is an argument about the care, the health record is like the referee's play-by-play — it is the main thing people look at to see what happened.

### Question 35

Your signature means 'I saw this and it is true' — you should not sign for something you did not see, just like you would not sign someone else's name on a report.

### Question 36

The assistant writes down what happened, while the doctor decides what it means — like an umpire calling what they saw while the coach decides the strategy.

### Question 37

A good late note says 'I am writing this now, about something from earlier' — it is honest about both times instead of faking the date.

### Question 38

If a record is found to contain lies, people stop believing the whole thing — like a storybook where one made-up part makes every page suspicious.

### Question 39

If a patient says something is missing, you tell the doctor so the doctor can check and write it the right way — you do not fill it in yourself.

### Question 40

An accurate record is like passing a clear, correct set of notes to the next shift — so the next person can keep things going safely.

### Question 41

If an important paper is missing, you tell the right person so it can be done properly — you do not fake a signature or a date.

### Question 42

If you are caught putting a fake date on one page, people will wonder if every other page is fake too — one lie makes the whole book suspect.

### Question 43

The audit trail is like a security camera over the record that notes who opened it, what they changed, and when they did it.

### Question 44

The audit trail is like a security camera that shows if anyone tried to sneak in and change the record without permission.

### Question 45

If you put a note in the wrong folder, you fix it the right way and tell a grown-up in charge — you do not pretend it never happened.

### Question 46

An addendum is like adding a correction slip to a notebook instead of ripping out the old page — the new note sits next to the original.

### Question 47

You cannot check off a chore as done when you have not done it yet — even if someone says you will do it later.

### Question 48

Safeguards are like locks and rules around a treasure chest — they keep the treasure private, unchanged, and there when it is needed.

### Question 49

Having your own login is like having your own locker key — only you should use it, so everyone knows whose actions are whose.

### Question 50

If two people use the same key, you cannot tell who opened the door — the same confusion happens with a shared login.

### Question 51

If you are not sure of a fact, you check first — like looking up the answer before writing it down instead of guessing.

### Question 52

Writing facts is like writing down the color you actually saw, not what you think the color should have been — facts can be double-checked.

### Question 53

When someone asks for their own report, you follow the office's rules to check it is really them before handing it over.

### Question 54

If your report has a mistake, the rules say you may ask for it to be fixed through a formal request — like asking a teacher to correct a grade.

### Question 55

If you are not sure a job is yours to do, ask a supervisor first — like checking with a teacher before doing something unfamiliar.

### Question 56

Each person writes their own part of the story, like each player writing their own part of a group report — so it matches what they really did.

### Question 57

You finish your own work, like writing your own part of a group project so it matches what you actually did.

### Question 58

Fixing a mistake the honest way — where people can see what was corrected — is better than hiding it, because hiding looks sneaky.

### Question 59

Sign with the real date you actually sign, and add an honest note if it was late — do not pretend you signed it earlier.

### Question 60

Writing lies in a health record can make a doctor give the wrong medicine later — the truth protects people, which is why it always matters.

### Question 61

Fix a wrong number the proper way so the computer shows both the old and new value — like keeping both the crossed-out answer and the new one.

### Question 62

The record is like a receipt — you can only ask to be paid for services that the receipt honestly shows were really given.

### Question 63

A strong record is like a complete, honest diary — written at the time, with all the facts, and signed by the person who wrote it.

### Question 64

A record with missing pieces is like a puzzle with holes — people fill the gaps with guesses, and those guesses can be wrong.

### Question 65

Writing care before it happens is like filling in a test answer before the question is asked — and if a friend does it, you tell the teacher.

### Question 66

If two pages of a story disagree, readers do not know which page to believe — so the whole story becomes less convincing.

### Question 67

If a mistake stays in the official notes, it needs to be fixed the right way — you keep telling the right people until it is.

### Question 68

The best fix is one where people can still see what was written first, like keeping the crossed-out answer next to the new one.

### Question 69

If two numbers disagree, check which one is right and fix the record the proper way — you do not just erase one to make them match.

### Question 70

A wrong tiny number in a recipe can ruin the whole dish — in medicine, a small wrong detail can lead to a big mistake in care.

### Question 71

Saying you taught someone when you did not is like telling the teacher you studied when you did not — later, everyone acts as if you knew it, and that can cause trouble.

### Question 72

The audit trail is like a security camera that names who touched the record, what they changed, and the exact time they did it.

### Question 73

You cannot tear a page out of an official record just because it is awkward — there is a formal way to ask for changes, and the doctor has to handle it.

### Question 74

A late note honestly says 'I am writing this now,' while backdating pretends it was written earlier — the difference is telling the truth about when.

### Question 75

If the record says a medicine was given but it was not, you fix the record and tell the nurse right away — so nobody gives it again by mistake.

### Question 76

It is like a rule that says 'if there is no receipt, there is no proof of the purchase' — so you keep the receipt, but you still actually buy the item.

### Question 77

Write down exactly what the person said and note that they said it — like quoting someone in a report instead of pretending you saw it yourself.

### Question 78

A proper change goes through official steps and keeps a record of what was there before — unlike sneaking in and erasing it.

### Question 79

If a friend leaves their locker open, you close it and tell them — you do not put your stuff in it or look through theirs.

### Question 80

Writing down the exact words and numbers a person says is like writing down the exact score — it is a fact, not your opinion about how it felt.

### Question 81

Filling in answers before the visit is like writing down test answers before the test starts — the answers are not real, and people may trust them anyway.

### Question 82

A record where corrections are clearly shown is more trustworthy than one that looks 'perfect' because mistakes were hidden — honesty beats a clean fake.

### Question 83

Passing an accurate record is like handing a detailed map to the next driver — without it, they might take a dangerous wrong turn.

### Question 84

If you did not see it yourself, say who told you — like writing 'my sister said' instead of pretending you saw it with your own eyes.

### Question 85

The record is like a careful, honest diary that both helps the patient stay healthy and proves what the office really did if anyone ever asks.
